title: Seva of the mind
hook: teaching, listening and sharing knowledge kindly are seva too

segments.voice: Yesterday, daswandh, the tenth share set aside first. Your line was a tenth, for others.

A neighbor who showed you how to change a tire. A coworker who, in your first week, quietly explained how things really work around here. A grandparent who taught a recipe without measuring anything. Somebody once taught you something small that stuck. No money changed hands. No dishes got washed. What they gave lives in your head now, and they may never have thought of it as a gift. Explaining something patiently, instead of sighing, is giving too. Sikhs have a name for that kind of giving, and it's the third of the three sevas.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SHOWED YOU HOW.` → `A GIFT THAT LIVES IN YOUR HEAD.` → `THE THIRD SEVA.`

segments.voice: Tan, dhan, and now man: the seva of the mind. Teaching what you know. Listening well. Sharing knowledge kindly, without making anyone feel small. You met a Guru who did this on day forty-five. Guru Angad took the Gurmukhi script and, tradition says, taught children to read it, so ordinary people could read the Gurus' words for themselves. That was seva of the mind on a grand scale: knowledge handed out, not locked up. Guru Nanak says in the Guru Granth Sahib, in paraphrase, that learning truly reflected on makes a person a benefactor of others. Knowledge that only makes you look clever hasn't finished its work. Knowledge that makes you useful has. The second half of this seva is listening. In the Japji, Guru Nanak gives four whole stanzas to listening, suniai, and says that by listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are erased. Listening is how you learn. But really listening to another person is also a gift you give. Someone who feels heard has been served. And one word matters here: kindly. Seva of the mind goes wrong when it turns into showing off, or correcting people so they feel stupid. The Sikh ideal is the opposite: humble, patient, glad to pass it on. Sikh communities do this in plain ways. Weekend Gurmukhi classes for children. Tutoring. Elders teaching the tunes of the hymns. Young people teaching elders how to use their phones. All of it counts. A mind can serve.
screen: `MAN — THE SEVA OF THE MIND.` · `ANGAD TEACHES CHILDREN TO READ.` · `LEARNING THAT HELPS OTHERS.` · `LISTENING IS A GIFT TOO.` · then, large: `GIVE WHAT YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you know how to do that someone near you doesn't: a computer shortcut, folding a fitted sheet, a word in another language, a way to calm down before a hard call. Picture showing it to someone who could use it, slowly, without making them feel slow, and notice how patience feels.
Man seva. Teaching, listening, and sharing what you know, kindly, so that others are served.
Your line: give what you know. Listening is giving too. Day one hundred one.

screen: `DAY 101 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHEN SEVA FEEDS THE EGO.`

howItsDone: Sikh communities run weekend Gurmukhi and kirtan classes, tutoring and study circles, and many Sikhs count teaching and patient listening as seva alongside cooking and giving.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think of' or tells the listener 'you've done it too'; the teach no longer points to the word 'kindly' in the hook, where it was never spoken.
Ang 356 (vidia vichari tan parupkari) paraphrased; confirm Ang and wording.
Japji stanzas 8-11 on suniai: 'sorrow and wrongdoing are erased' paraphrases the refrain (dukh pap ka nas). Confirm.
Guru Angad and Gurmukhi: tradition credits him with standardizing and teaching the script; historians debate its earlier origins. Stated as tradition; consistent with day 45.
'Third of the three sevas' refers to the order taught (hands, purse, mind), matching days 99-101.
